title: Why Do Cats Purr?
description: Science still has no settled answer, but the leading ideas are strange, and one purr hides a cry aimed at you.
question: Why do cats purr?

facts.claim: No one knows for sure why domestic cats purr; the function is still unsettled.
facts.note: Library of Congress answer, plus veterinary behaviorist Benjamin Hart at a 2010 AVMA session. The video should present the reasons below as leading ideas, not a single proven answer.

facts.claim: A cat's purr is very low-pitched, reaching down to about 25 Hz.
facts.note: Sources disagree on the upper limit: AAHA and Scientific American give 25-150 Hz, while Herbst et al. describe a purr regime of 25-30 Hz. About 25 Hz is the point these sources share, so avoid showing 25-150 Hz as settled.

facts.claim: Cats purr on both the in-breath and the out-breath, with purring sequences alternating between the two.
The study showing cat larynges can make purring frequencies without neural input was published in Current Biology in 2023.
facts.note: Herbst et al., Current Biology 33(21): 4727-4732, published November 6, 2023.

facts.claim: Researchers tested larynges removed from eight domestic cats, and all eight produced self-sustained purring-rate oscillations.
facts.note: Ex vivo work: warm, humidified air was passed through excised larynges. It was not done in living cats.

facts.claim: With only airflow and no nerve signals or muscle contraction, the excised cat larynges produced sounds at 25 to 30 Hz.
Connective tissue masses up to 4 mm in diameter are embedded in cats' vocal folds and may help explain the unusually low frequency of purring.
facts.note: The pads are observed anatomy, but their role in lowering pitch is a proposal. Use 'may' on screen.

facts.claim: The 2023 data do not fully rule out the older idea that brain-driven muscle contractions help produce the purr in living cats.
facts.note: Avoid saying the brain plays no part in purring. The study shows the larynx can produce purring frequencies without neural input, not that living cats purr that way.

facts.claim: The study identifying a cry-like signal inside cats' food-soliciting purrs was published in Current Biology in 2009.
facts.note: McComb, Taylor, Wilson and Charlton, Current Biology 19: R507-R508. One blog dates it to 2015, but the volume number and press coverage confirm 2009.

facts.claim: Cats soliciting food can embed a high-frequency voiced element inside the low-pitched purr.
facts.note: The authors suggest it may exploit a mammalian sensitivity to cries. The comparison to a human baby's cry is an interpretation, not a demonstrated fact.

facts.claim: The cry-like element in solicitation purrs peaks between 220 and 520 Hz, far above the purr's low rumble.
facts.note: Taken from press coverage of McComb et al.; the figure was not checked against the paper's full text. Coverage also reports a mean of 380 Hz.

facts.claim: People rate food-soliciting purrs as more urgent and less pleasant than purrs made in other situations.
When researchers digitally removed the embedded cry from recorded purrs, listeners' urgency ratings dropped significantly.
facts.note: Press coverage of McComb et al.

facts.claim: Veterinarians suggest kittens' purring tells their mother 'I am okay' and 'I am here', and purring is linked to nursing and mother-kitten bonding.
facts.note: Pet-care sites often say kittens first purr at about two days old, but no primary source was found, so that number is deliberately left out.

facts.claim: Purring doesn't always mean happiness: many cats also purr when afraid or in pain, which may be a form of self-soothing.
facts.value: also purr in fear or pain
facts.note: That cats purr in these situations is well reported by veterinarians. The self-soothing explanation, including AAHA's suggestion of endorphin release, remains a hypothesis.

facts.claim: The idea that purring helps cats heal is unproven: purr frequencies overlap those studied for bone healing, but no direct studies show purring itself heals fractures.
facts.note: AAHA's article links these frequencies to tissue repair more confidently, while Tufts says the question is still debated, so frame this only as a hypothesis. The popular '30% stronger bones' figure appears to come from vibration-therapy research, not purring, and should not be used.
